hook.text: A song goes viral not because it's the best — but because enough people already listened to it.

buildup.text: The bandwagon effect is our tendency to adopt beliefs and behaviors proportional to others doing the same.

discovery.text: In an experiment, artificial download counts made random songs chart-toppers. Popularity created more popularity.

twist.text: This creates winner-take-all dynamics. Early momentum matters more than actual quality.

climax.text: Political polls, bestseller lists, and trending hashtags all trigger bandwagon cascades that self-reinforce.

punchline.text: The popular choice isn't always the best. It's the first.

quiz.question: What drives the bandwagon effect?
options: People adopting behaviors others have adopted

details.summary: The bandwagon effect drives people to adopt beliefs and behaviors simply because others have. As momentum builds, the perceived popularity becomes self-reinforcing. Trends, political movements, and product adoption all exhibit this cascade pattern.
details.whyItMatters: Bandwagon dynamics explain everything from viral trends to election momentum. Recognizing this effect helps you evaluate ideas on merit rather than popularity.
takeaways: Popularity itself becomes a reason for adoption
The effect accelerates in social media environments

faq.question: How is the bandwagon effect different from social proof?
faq.answer: Social proof uses evidence of others' behavior to inform decisions. The bandwagon effect specifically describes joining because of momentum and popularity regardless of evidence. Social proof can be informative; the bandwagon effect is primarily emotional and tribal.

faq.question: Can the bandwagon effect reverse suddenly?
faq.answer: Yes. When a critical mass of people defect or a prominent figure publicly abandons a trend, cascading abandonment can be just as rapid as adoption. Financial bubbles popping and sudden brand boycotts both demonstrate how quickly bandwagons can reverse.
